tldr: We propose AIRoA-0, a foundation model that uses zero physical robot data and trains solely on 16,151 hours of human handheld gripper data. Using only wrist-mounted cameras, it autonomously performs long-horizon, precise bimanual manipulation tasks.
hero_caption: Overview of AIRoA-0. Trained entirely on human demonstrations recorded with a handheld gripper (YUBI), it operates diverse robots—such as Franka, the humanoid TX-G2, the open-source OpenArm, and UR arms—out-of-the-box using only sensory input from dual wrist cameras.
overview:
The primary bottleneck in robot learning is the cost of collecting real robot data. Collecting data via robot teleoperation is bound to specific robot hardware and physical locations, making it extremely difficult to scale up. Recently, an alternative approach has gained significant attention: humans demonstrate tasks using handheld grippers (such as UMI) while recording video and end-effector trajectories. This approach can scale concurrently anywhere as long as human demonstrators are available.

However, handheld data faces major hurdles. It contains no visual appearance of robot arms or examples of failure and recovery. Furthermore, visual observations are limited to local views from two wrist-mounted cameras, making it easy to lose track of progress across long-horizon tasks. Generalization is also severely challenged because collection environments and deployment sites differ completely.

AIRoA-0 (A-0), proposed in this paper, overcomes these challenges through an end-to-end system design. Using a massive 16,151-hour dataset collected with the open-source handheld gripper "YUBI," the authors designed pre-training and post-training pipelines. The system integrates a visual attention mechanism that filters out irrelevant backgrounds, a stage prediction head that predicts task progression, a proprioceptive memory that retains recent arm motions, and non-uniform streaming decoding that generates smooth real-time execution.

Across 10 bimanual tasks evaluated in unseen deployment environments, A-0 achieved an average success rate of 78%, substantially outperforming state-of-the-art vision-language-action (VLA) baselines whose best performer achieved only 27%. Without any real-robot data collection or reinforcement learning, it demonstrates the ability to complete multi-minute precision tasks—such as replacing robot vacuum brushes and mop pads—from a single language instruction.
contributions: Built AIRoA-0, a bimanual manipulation system pre-trained and post-trained entirely on 16,151 hours of handheld gripper data without using any real robot data.

Completely open-sourced one of the world's largest handheld datasets with task- and subtask-level language annotations, pre-trained weights, post-training recipes, and both hardware and software designs for the YUBI handheld gripper.
Demonstrated that a robot can execute long-horizon, precise bimanual tasks from a single prompt in unseen target environments using only two wrist cameras and no overhead camera.

Achieved embodiment independence by adopting an end-effector-relative coordinate frame (Anchored actions), enabling zero-shot deployment across diverse platforms—including Franka, TX-G2, OpenArm, and UR—without retraining or tuning model weights.

sections.heading: Operating Robots from 16,000 Hours of Data Collected Without Robots
sections.summary: We developed AIRoA-0 (A-0), a bimanual system that tackles long-horizon, high-precision tasks trained exclusively on human demonstrations collected via handheld grippers, without real robot data. An integrated modeling and control design overcomes severe constraints: a narrow field of view from dual wrist cameras and deployment to completely unseen environments.
sections.details:
When teaching tasks to robots, collecting data on physical platforms is constrained by hardware availability and physical locations. In contrast, handheld data collection—where humans perform tasks holding grippers in both hands—can scale linearly with the number of human demonstrators.

However, this data lacks robot-specific motion dynamics and recovery behaviors. Without overhead cameras providing global context, policies must track long task procedures using only narrow fields of view from two wrist cameras. Additionally, policies trained on data collected across diverse homes and offices must generalize to target deployment sites never seen during training.

A-0 overcomes all of these hurdles. Both pre-training and post-training are completed exclusively with handheld data, requiring neither reinforcement learning nor on-robot trajectory corrections. Despite this, it completes multi-minute tasks requiring millimeter-level contact precision—such as unzipping pencil cases, folding towels, and servicing robot vacuum components—guided by a single-sentence language prompt.

Across 10 evaluated bimanual tasks, A-0 achieved an average success rate of 78%, far outperforming existing strong VLA baselines (which capped at 27%). By designing the handheld gripper to mount directly onto robot arms as their end-effector, the exact same pre-trained weights drive structurally diverse platforms, from Franka arms to the humanoid TX-G2 and industrial UR manipulators.

sections.heading: Dominant Performance Across 10 Long-Horizon Tasks and Instant Adaptation to Disturbances
sections.summary: In an unseen environment with zero training data, A-0 was tested across 10 bimanual tasks, achieving a dominant average success rate of 78% over strong baselines. It also demonstrated smooth trajectory adjustments and real-time adaptation when sudden human disturbances were introduced, such as moving sorting bins during execution.
sections.details:
### 2.1. Physical Robot Evaluations Across 10 Tasks
We evaluated 10 tasks on a dual-arm Franka setup in an experimental environment where no training demonstrations had been collected. We compared A-0 against four state-of-the-art open-source VLA models: $\pi_{0.5}$, Xiaomi-Robotics-1 (XR-1), GR00T N1.7, and MolmoAct2. While these baselines used optimal task-specific hyperparameter configurations found via grid searches over action horizons and control frequencies, A-0 applied a single, shared post-training recipe (hyperparameters) across all tasks.

As a result, while the baselines achieved average success rates between 14% and 27%, A-0 reached an average of 78%, ranking first across all 10 tasks. Post-training data efficiency was also notable, requiring only 3 to 6 hours of demonstrations per task. In the robot vacuum maintenance task, A-0 seamlessly completed an over-two-minute complex workflow—peeling off two used mop pads, discarding them into a bin, mounting two fresh pads, and unlatching the main brush—prompted by just one initial instruction.

### 2.2. Robustness to Dynamic Environmental Disturbances
Although A-0's training data contains no disturbance scenarios, it reacts promptly to visual changes captured by its wrist cameras. In a bolt color-sorting task, when a human suddenly shifted the sorting box sideways while the arm was already descending, the robot smoothly redirected its trajectory and dropped the bolt into the relocated bin. Furthermore, when the arrangement of the boxes was swapped mid-action, the policy visually tracked the target color and continued sorting correctly.

### 2.3. Cross-Embodiment Verification Across Diverse Platforms
Because A-0 represents states and actions relative to the robot's end-effector (gripper), it can be deployed on any robot that accommodates the YUBI gripper. Beyond dual-arm Franka, we validated operation on three other platforms: the humanoid TX-G2, the low-cost open-source OpenArm, and an industrial UR arm. Remarkably, without any embodiment-specific fine-tuning or parameter adjustments, the exact same model weights successfully performed tasks like cup stacking and zipper opening across all platforms.

captions.F2: The 10 bimanual tasks used for evaluation. They cover demanding challenges requiring high-precision contact and extended execution sequences, such as towel folding, letter block alignment, orange pyramid stacking, and part sorting.
captions.F3: Autonomous execution of the robot vacuum cleaner maintenance task. The robot autonomously completes the entire sequence uncut in about two minutes: detaching two used mop pads, retrieving and mounting fresh pads from a box, and removing the main brush.
captions.F4: Response to sudden human disturbance during the color sorting task. While transporting a green part in (a), the bin is abruptly pushed left in (b). The arm does not pause or hesitate; it drops the part into the relocated green bin through a single smooth trajectory in (c) and (d).
captions.F5: A-0 operating across different robot embodiments. Using the identical model weights, it achieves precise bimanual manipulation on the humanoid TX-G2 (top), the low-cost OpenArm, and the industrial UR manipulator (bottom).

sections.heading: A Massive 16,000-Hour, 10-Million-Step Bimanual Handheld Dataset
sections.summary: Using "YUBI," a handheld gripper that links finger movements while recording wrist camera views and 6-DoF poses, we constructed a 16,151-hour bimanual manipulation corpus. All data is annotated with a two-tiered language structure consisting of task-level instructions and second-level subtask prompts.
sections.details:
### 3.1. The Handheld Gripper: YUBI
YUBI is an open-source handheld data collection tool developed for scalable gathering of demonstrations. Its jaws mirror human finger open-close motions, wrist-mounted cameras capture ego-centric visual observations, and external tracking systems precisely record 6-DoF poses. Human operators simply hold YUBIs in both hands and perform manual tasks naturally, simultaneously recording wrist camera streams, hand trajectories, and gripper states. When YUBI is directly mounted as the robot's end-effector, the visual perspectives and motion trajectories experienced by the robot match the human demonstration data perfectly.

### 3.2. Corpus Scope and Two-Tiered Language Annotations
The collected corpus totals 16,151 hours, spanning over 100 diverse bimanual tasks (pick-and-place, sorting, assembly, cable routing, tool use, handovers, and more).

A central feature of this dataset is its two-tiered language labeling, consisting of overall "task instructions" alongside short "subtask instructions" covering segments of just a few seconds. For example, for the task instruction "service the robot vacuum cleaner," detailed subtask labels such as "remove the first mop pad and place it in the box" and "detach the action brush" are annotated across 10.65 million segments. This structured language grounding plays a crucial role during subsequent pre-training and post-training.

sections.heading: Pre-Training: Learning Where to Look and Scaling with Data Volume
sections.summary: Based on $\pi_{0.5}$, pre-training integrates end-effector-relative coordinates (Anchored actions) and an attention gating mechanism that limits visual information budgets. Scaling handheld data reveals that downstream post-training loss decreases cleanly following a power law.
sections.details:
### 4.1. Model Architecture and 4.2. Anchored Actions
A-0 builds upon $\pi_{0.5}$ (SigLIP vision encoder, Gemma 2B language backbone, and a 300M action expert based on Flow Matching). Inputs consist of dual wrist-camera images ($224\times 224$), language instructions, and proprioceptive states (11-dimensional relative poses and gripper widths for both hands). Outputs are action chunks of 32 future steps sampled on a 20Hz grid.

A key innovation is the "Anchored actions" relative coordinate representation. Each action step is defined as a relative transformation anchored to the gripper's pose at the current observation timestamp. This eliminates robot-specific coordinates such as base frames and joint angles that cannot be shared between humans and robots, ensuring identical numerical representations whether held by a human or mounted on a robot. Furthermore, because each future step is an independent target relative to the current observation pose, errors do not compound over time, making trajectories easier for low-level robot controllers to track.

### 4.3. Two-Tiered Language and 4.4. Visual Evidence Budget Gate
During pre-training, either a task-level or subtask-level instruction is provided as a prompt at random. To eliminate irrelevant background clutter from the wrist cameras, we introduced an S2 (See Less, Specify More) framework. A lightweight scoring network evaluates the relevance of each image token to the language instruction, computing a retention probability $m_p$. Constraining the mean retention probability to a budget target $\rho$ via a budget loss forces the model to focus purely on manipulation targets and the gripper while ignoring background desks and room scenery, all without needing bounding-box annotations.

### 4.5. Subtask Auxiliary Loss and 4.6. Pre-Training Data Scaling
When given a task instruction, the model is trained with an auxiliary loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{sub}}$ to predict the active subtask name as text from current observations. This encourages the backbone to naturally develop internal representations of overall task progress.

Scaling pre-training data from 6.25% up to 100% showed steady reductions in validation loss. Furthermore, evaluating post-training loss across unseen target tasks revealed a clear power law: $L = 0.063\,D^{-0.035}$ ($R^2=0.98$) with respect to pre-training hours $D$. Doubling pre-training data improved post-training task loss by approximately 2.4%, proving that large-scale handheld data collection directly enhances robot manipulation performance.

captions.F8: Visualization of regions prioritized by the Visual Budget Gate. Across 25 subtasks, the model naturally fades out task-irrelevant backgrounds and tables, concentrating its attention on the active gripper and grasped objects.

sections.heading: Stage Prediction and Short-Term Proprioceptive Memory for Downstream Adaptation
sections.summary: During task-specific post-training, we introduce a stage prediction head that classifies the ongoing execution phase and a proprioceptive memory that compresses the last 10 motion steps. Using a single uniform training recipe across all tasks, post-training finishes in under 4 hours on a single 8x H200 GPU node.
sections.details:
### 5.1. Tracking Progress via Stage Prediction
Because wrist cameras capture only local visual observations, determining the current global progress stage visually can often be ambiguous. To resolve this, A-0 partitions tasks into sequential stages and incorporates a classification head that predicts the current stage from observations. The predicted stage is fed directly as text into the action expert, which was already pre-trained to follow subtask prompts. This allows the policy to select correct downstream actions without getting lost in long-horizon sequences.

### 5.2. Proprioceptive Memory
Single-frame observations cannot convey the direction in which the robot arm was moving immediately prior. We therefore introduced a mechanism that compresses the history of the past 10 end-effector poses and timestamps into four learnable query tokens via attention, feeding them directly into the prompt. To handle varying control loop frequencies across physical setups, historical timesteps are randomly sampled between 5 and 15Hz during training, with history masked out 25% of the time to ensure robustness if memory is unavailable.

### 5.3. Visual Budget Gate in Post-Training and 5.4. Fast Training via a Single Recipe
The Visual Budget Gate remains active during post-training. In addition to filtering image tokens, the gate's retention probabilities are injected as a prior attention bias into the cross-attention layers of the action generation head.

The overall post-training loss combines the Flow Matching action loss, stage prediction loss, visual budget loss, and subtask auxiliary loss. Importantly, all 10 tasks in this paper were trained using the exact same post-training recipe without any task-specific hyperparameter tuning. On a single compute node equipped with 8x H200 GPUs, post-training for any task completes in under 4 hours.

sections.heading: Non-Uniform Streaming Decoding Balances Smoothness and Responsiveness
sections.summary: To eliminate jerky motions and latency during on-robot inference, we propose exponential moving average filtering on predicted stages alongside a novel non-uniform streaming decoding scheme. This removes discontinuities between action chunks while preserving rapid ~60ms reactivity to dynamic changes.
sections.details:
### 6.1. Stage EMA Smoothing
Because stage predictions are generated every step from partial visual observations, momentary misclassifications can occur. At inference time, we apply an exponential moving average (EMA) to the predicted class probabilities. This prevents sudden spikes in incorrect actions caused by transient visual noise, ensuring smooth, natural transitions as the task progresses.

### 6.2. Non-Uniform Streaming Decoding
Standard Flow Matching generates action chunks by running around 10 denoising steps from pure noise, which is computationally expensive and tends to introduce motion discontinuities at chunk boundaries. Conversely, uniform streaming schemes (such as FlashVLA) that recycle noise buffers across fixed slots face a dilemma: small buffer sizes leave visible boundary seams, while larger buffer sizes cause the arm to lag behind environmental changes due to stale observations.

To solve this, the authors propose a non-uniform noise schedule that assigns smaller update steps to actions closer to execution. A-0 employs two buffer slots with noise levels set to $(0.1, 1.0)$. A freshly inserted chunk is coarsely denoised from 1.0 down to 0.1, while the chunk about to be executed in the next step receives only a fine-grained correction from 0.1 down to 0 conditioned on the freshest observation.

This design ensures smooth trajectory transitions between chunks while allowing the policy to react instantly when a human moves target objects mid-motion. Requiring zero extra model parameters and only two function evaluations in steady state, it achieves exceptionally fast on-robot inference of ~60ms (~16Hz) on an H200 GPU.

sections.heading: Breaking Long-Horizon Barriers by Combining Handheld Collection with VLAs
sections.summary: We review prior literature on handheld data collection (e.g., UMI), VLA foundation models like $\pi_{0}$, and real-time action generation. A-0 fuses these paradigms to achieve long-horizon, high-precision bimanual manipulation under the most scalable paradigm: zero robot data and wrist cameras only.
sections.details:
Data collection with handheld grippers was pioneered by UMI and expanded by works like Dobb-E and HiFi-UMI. Because it eliminates the need for physical robots and scales with human operators, it is ideal for capturing diverse environments and objects. A-0 builds upon this foundation, scaling collection up to 16,151 hours and extending its capabilities to long-horizon bimanual manipulation.

Architecturally, A-0 aligns with advances in VLAs such as RT-2, OpenVLA, and $\pi_{0.5}$. While most prior works rely on robot teleoperation data or online reinforcement learning corrections, A-0 focuses purely on zero-shot embodiment transfer from handheld demonstrations without using a single second of physical robot data.

To prevent the loss of context in long-horizon tasks, A-0 refines language-intermediate approaches seen in RT-H and Hi Robot into a lightweight, reliable stage prediction head. For real-time execution, it builds upon streaming methods from Diffusion Policy and FlashVLA, introducing a non-uniform noise schedule that achieves both trajectory smoothness and immediate responsiveness to disturbances.

sections.heading: A New Standard Path for Robot Learning: From Handheld Data to Physical Execution
sections.summary: AIRoA-0 demonstrates that long-horizon, high-precision bimanual manipulation can be learned entirely from handheld data without collecting any robot demonstrations. Open-sourcing the dataset, model weights, training recipes, and hardware designs provides an accessible environment for anyone to train custom tasks rapidly.
sections.details:
A-0 is a unified system engineered consistently across all layers: tool hardware design, data pre-processing, pre-training, post-training, and inference execution harness. It proves that demanding contact-rich manipulation can be executed from a single instruction using only two wrist cameras in deployment environments unseen during training.

Furthermore, the work offers exceptional reproducibility and openness. The 16,151-hour dataset, pre-trained model weights, unified post-training recipe, and 3D CAD files and collection software for the YUBI gripper are all publicly released. Researchers and engineers can fabricate the gripper from open designs, record a few hours of demonstration data, and obtain an autonomous policy on a GPU node in under 4 hours.

takeaways: High-precision bimanual manipulation policies can be built entirely from human handheld data without using any physical robot data or reinforcement learning, provided Anchored actions and an appropriate system design are used.
Handheld data collection time and downstream post-training loss follow a clear power-law scaling relationship, proving that the model consistently improves as more data is gathered.

Combining a Visual Budget Gate (which filters out irrelevant background clutter from wrist cameras) with a stage prediction head (which tracks overall progress) is highly effective for mastering long-horizon tasks.
Non-uniform streaming decoding reduces Flow Matching computational overhead while simultaneously eliminating chunk-boundary discontinuities and enabling instant adaptation to dynamic disturbances.
limitations: Deployment is restricted to robots that can directly mount the YUBI handheld gripper as their end-effector; direct transfer to hands or grippers with different kinematic mechanisms remains unverified.
Because the system relies solely on wrist-mounted cameras without overhead or global views, it cannot support wide-area visual search or mobile navigation beyond the reach of the arms.

Each new task still requires a few hours of task-specific post-training; the system has not yet reached zero-shot generalization capable of executing completely novel tasks directly from language instructions.
